title: Introduction to Medical Virology — Lecture I
summary: Viruses are obligate intracellular submicroscopic infectious agents that replicate only inside living cells and can infect animal, plant, bacterial, and protozoal cells.

The term virus comes from Latin and means poison or toxic fluid; the discovery history begins with Dmitri Ivanovsky's 1892 tobacco-mosaic-virus filtration experiment and Martinus Beijerinck's 1898 interpretation.
Three hypotheses have been proposed for virus origin: regressive, escape/progressive, and co-evolution/virus-first; none has been clearly confirmed to date.
Viruses are classified according to size, structure, genome, physical properties, chemical properties, and target tissue.
Viral particles contain a core and capsid, with an envelope present in some viruses and matrix protein in enveloped viruses; capsid plus nucleic-acid core forms the nucleocapsid.
The viral genome contains either DNA or RNA, not both, and may be single- or double-stranded, linear or circular, and segmented or non-segmented.
The capsid protects viral nucleic acid, participates in delivery into host cells through attachment proteins, determines antigenic characteristics, and determines viral symmetry.
Major viral symmetry patterns are icosahedral, helical, and complex. Viral envelopes are lipoprotein structures whose lipid portion is derived from host membranes.

Physical and chemical stability varies with heat, cold, dryness, ultraviolet radiation, ether/chloroform, glycerol, formaldehyde, chlorine, and iodine. Target-cell specificity is described by viral tropism.

Viral replication proceeds through adsorption, penetration, uncoating, synthesis of viral macromolecules, assembly, and release; viral particles may be complete, defective, pseudoviruses, or coreless, while subviral agents include prions and viroids.

keyTerms.definition: An agent that requires a living host cell for replication and cannot thrive and reproduce outside the living cell.
The term used by Martinus Beijerinck for the filtered infectious agent; infectious, living, fluid.
The hypothesis that viruses began as small pre-virus cells that lost metabolic and reproductive abilities and became dependent on host-cell pathways.
The capsid together with the viral nucleic-acid core.
The ability of a virus to specifically infect a particular cell, tissue, or host that supports its replication.
The phase during viral macromolecule synthesis when no viral particles can be detected inside the infected host cell.
A premature virus with an incomplete genome that can require a helper virus for replication.
A small proteinaceous infectious particle made of misfolded protein without detected nucleic acid.

flashcards.front: Why are viruses called obligate intracellular agents?
flashcards.back: They replicate only inside living cells because they cannot thrive and reproduce outside the living cell.

flashcards.front: Who first discovered the infectious agent later identified as tobacco mosaic virus?
flashcards.back: Dmitri Ivanovsky in 1892, after filtration of infected tobacco-plant extracts.

flashcards.front: What did Beijerinck call the new infectious agent?
What are the three hypotheses for virus origin?

flashcards.back: The capsid plus the nucleic-acid core.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between +sense and -sense RNA?
flashcards.back: +sense RNA acts as mRNA and is directly translated; -sense RNA acts as a template for mRNA synthesis first.

flashcards.front: What are the three viral symmetry types?
What are the two main methods of viral release?

questions.question: Which statement best defines viruses according to the lecture?
options: They are free-living microorganisms that reproduce on ordinary culture media
They are obligate intracellular submicroscopic infectious agents that replicate only inside living cells
They are protein-only particles that infect plants exclusively
They are bacteria that have lost their cell walls
questions.explanation: The lecture defines viruses as obligate intracellular submicroscopic infectious agents that replicate only inside living cells.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Viruses require living cells for replication.
Correct. This matches the lecture definition.
Incorrect. Prions are proteinaceous subviral agents, while viruses infect many types of cells.
Incorrect. Viruses are not bacteria lacking cell walls.
questions.hint: Focus on the requirement for a living cell.

questions.question: Why did Ivanovsky's filtration experiment suggest that the tobacco-mosaic infectious agent was not an ordinary bacterium?
options: The agent grew rapidly on ordinary culture media
The infectious filtrate passed through a Chamberland filter that normally retains bacteria and fungi
The agent was easily seen by the light microscope
The agent became noninfectious after filtration
questions.explanation: Ivanovsky found that the filtrate remained infectious after passage through a Chamberland filter that normally retains bacteria and fungi.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Growth on ordinary culture media was not the key observation.
Correct. Continued infectivity after filtration was the key finding.
Incorrect. The lecture does not identify that as the discovery basis.
Incorrect. The filtrate remained infectious.
questions.hint: Remember what the Chamberland filter normally retains.

questions.question: Who repeated Ivanovsky's experiment in 1898 and used the term 'contagium vivum fluidum'?
questions.explanation: Martinus Beijerinck repeated the experiment in 1898 and described the filtered infectious agent as contagium vivum fluidum.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Ivanovsky performed the earlier 1892 experiment.
Incorrect. Prusiner coined the term prion in 1982.
Correct. Beijerinck made the 1898 interpretation.
Incorrect. Pasteur is not identified here as the scientist who named the agent.
questions.hint: Think of the 1898 scientist.

questions.question: Which hypothesis proposes that viruses arose from small cells that lost metabolic and reproductive abilities?
questions.explanation: The regressive hypothesis proposes that pre-virus cells lost metabolic and reproductive abilities and became dependent on host-cell pathways.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Escape involves mobile genetic elements leaving their original cellular environment.
Incorrect. Co-evolution proposes evolution before or alongside the host cell.
Correct. This is the regressive/reduction hypothesis.
Incorrect. Capsid mispackaging is related to pseudovirus formation.
questions.hint: Look for the theory involving reduction or loss of functions.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a criterion for classification of viruses?
questions.explanation: The listed criteria are size, structure, genome, physical properties, chemical properties, and target tissue.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Genome is listed.
Incorrect. Target tissue is listed.
Incorrect. Physical properties are listed.
Correct. Antibiotic susceptibility is not listed.
questions.hint: Review the six classification criteria.

questions.question: According to the lecture, viruses generally range in size from approximately:
questions.explanation: The lecture states that viruses range from about 20 to 400 nm; giant viruses can exceed 400 nm.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is below the stated range.
Correct. This is the general range given.
Incorrect. This is not the stated general range.
Incorrect. The lecture gives the unit as nanometers.
questions.hint: Remember the unit as well as the endpoints.

questions.question: Which method determines viral size indirectly using a collodion membrane of graded porosity?
questions.explanation: Ultrafiltration uses a collodion membrane with graded pore sizes to estimate viral size.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Electron microscopy directly determines size.
Incorrect. Ultracentrifugation uses sedimentation rate.
Correct. This is the collodion membrane method.
Incorrect. Light microscopy is not the method described.
questions.hint: Think about the membrane-filter method.

questions.question: Which statement about basic viral structure is correct?
options: Every virus has an envelope and matrix protein
The nucleocapsid consists of the capsid plus the nucleic-acid core
The capsid is made only of host phospholipids
The viral genome is always outside the capsid
questions.explanation: The lecture defines the nucleocapsid as capsid plus nucleic-acid core. Envelope and matrix protein occur only in enveloped viruses.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Not every virus is enveloped.
Correct. This is the lecture's definition of nucleocapsid.
Incorrect. The capsid is a protein coat.
Incorrect. The viral genome is enclosed by the capsid.
questions.hint: Recall the definition of nucleocapsid.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the viral genome?
options: It contains both DNA and RNA in every virus
It contains either DNA or RNA, not both
questions.explanation: The viral genome contains either DNA or RNA, not both. Either type may be single- or double-stranded.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The lecture explicitly says DNA or RNA, not both.
Correct. This is the central statement about viral genome composition.
Incorrect. DNA viral genomes can be single- or double-stranded.
Incorrect. RNA genomes can also be double-stranded.
questions.hint: The key phrase is DNA OR RNA.

questions.question: A positive-sense RNA viral genome is one that:
options: Must first be converted to DNA before translation
Acts as mRNA and is directly translated to protein
Cannot serve as a template for protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Positive-sense RNA acts as mRNA and is directly translated into protein.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is not the lecture's definition of positive-sense RNA.
Correct. Positive-sense RNA functions directly as mRNA.
Incorrect. It is directly translated.
Incorrect. Sense refers to coding orientation, not strand number.
questions.hint: Positive-sense RNA behaves like mRNA.

questions.question: Which is a function of the viral capsid?
options: Protecting viral nucleic acid from nucleases
Supplying all ATP for viral replication
questions.explanation: Protection of the viral nucleic acid from nucleases is one of the four capsid functions listed in the lecture.
optionExplanations: Correct. The lecture explicitly lists protection from nucleases.
Incorrect. ATP is supplied by the host cell.
Incorrect. Host ribosomes remain necessary for protein synthesis.
Incorrect. The capsid is not a universal anti-mutation mechanism.
questions.hint: Think of the capsid's protective role.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes icosahedral viral symmetry?
options: Capsomers and genome are twisted into a spiral tube
It results from twenty equilateral triangles and provides a highly rigid structure
It has no defined capsomer arrangement
It occurs only in enveloped RNA viruses
questions.explanation: The lecture describes icosahedral symmetry as an arrangement of twenty equilateral triangles that provides a highly rigid structure.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. A spiral tube describes helical symmetry.
Correct. This matches the lecture's description.
Incorrect. Complex symmetry is the one without icosahedral or helical orientation.
Incorrect. The lecture does not restrict icosahedral symmetry this way.
questions.hint: Think of the 20 triangular faces of an icosahedron.

questions.question: Which pairing is correctly matched?
options: Helical symmetry — capsomers and genome twist together; Orthomyxoviridae is an example
Complex symmetry — twenty equilateral triangular faces
Icosahedral symmetry — capsomers and genome form a spiral tube
questions.explanation: The lecture defines helical symmetry as capsomers and genome twisted together and lists Orthomyxoviridae as an example.
optionExplanations: Correct. This matches the lecture.
Incorrect. Twenty triangles describe icosahedral symmetry.
Incorrect. The spiral tube describes helical symmetry.
Incorrect. Complex symmetry is exemplified by poxvirus and bacteriophage.
questions.hint: Match the geometry to the description.

questions.question: The viral envelope is composed of:
options: Lipoproteins, with lipid derived from host membrane and protein encoded by viral nucleic acid
questions.explanation: The lecture states that the envelope is a lipoprotein structure: host membrane provides the lipid portion, while the viral genome encodes the protein portion.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Nucleic acid forms the viral genome, not the envelope.
Correct. This is the lecture's description of envelope composition.
Incorrect. Carbohydrates are not the described main structure.
Incorrect. Capsomers form the capsid.
questions.hint: Remember host-derived lipid plus virus-encoded protein.

questions.question: Which statement about heat sensitivity is correct according to the lecture?
options: Enveloped viruses are generally heat sensitive while non-enveloped viruses are more heat resistant
All viruses are immediately destroyed by cold storage
Non-enveloped viruses are always heat sensitive
Most viruses are most unstable at -70 °C
questions.explanation: The lecture states that enveloped viruses are heat sensitive while non-enveloped viruses are heat resistant. It also notes that most viruses are stable at -40 to -70 °C.
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the lecture's heat classification.
Incorrect. Most viruses are stable at -40 to -70 °C.
Incorrect. The lecture gives the opposite comparison.
Incorrect. The lecture says most viruses are stable in that cold range.
questions.hint: Compare enveloped with non-enveloped viruses under heat.

questions.question: What is the main function of the viral genome?
What is the capsid?
options: An impermeable protein shell around viral nucleic acid

questions.question: What are capsomers?
options: Protein subunits composed of polypeptide molecules

questions.question: Which is NOT a listed function of the viral capsid?
options: Delivery of viral nucleic acid into the host cell

questions.question: What does viral symmetry describe?
options: The morphological shape of the viral capsid based on the arrangement of capsomers
The age of the host cell
The temperature required for viral replication
The length of the viral genome only

questions.question: Which set contains all three types of viral symmetry described in the lecture?
How many equilateral triangles are involved in the icosahedral arrangement described in the lecture?
In the icosahedral symmetry described in the lecture, what are the protein subunits at the angles of each triangular capsomer called?
How are the capsomers and viral genome arranged in helical symmetry?
options: They are twisted together to form a helical or spiral tube
They are completely separated from each other
They are located only inside the nucleus
They are absent from RNA viruses

questions.question: Which virus was given as an example of complex viral symmetry?
What is the lipid portion of the viral envelope mainly derived from?
What are the protein spikes projecting from the viral envelope also called?
Which function of the viral envelope is directly related to binding to specific receptors on a host cell?
Which of the following is another function of the viral envelope?
options: Evasion of the host immune system

questions.question: Which set contains possible sources of viral envelopes inside the host cell?
options: Plasma membrane, nuclear membrane, Golgi apparatus membrane, and endoplasmic reticulum

questions.question: Most viruses can be inactivated by heating at 56 °C for approximately:
Most viruses are stable at approximately which temperature range?
Which virus was described in the lecture as unable to survive longer than 8 hours on hard dry surfaces?
Which genome types are less susceptible to ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI) than ssDNA and ssRNA viruses?
Which statement about ether and chloroform is correct?
options: Non-enveloped viruses are sensitive to both
Both enveloped and non-enveloped viruses are always resistant
Enveloped viruses are sensitive, while non-enveloped viruses are resistant

questions.question: Which statement correctly matches a chemical agent with viral sensitivity?
options: Enveloped viruses are sensitive to ether and chloroform
Glycerol destroys viruses and is used as a virucide
Viruses are resistant to formaldehyde, chlorine, and iodine
Non-enveloped viruses are more ether sensitive than enveloped viruses
questions.explanation: The lecture states that enveloped viruses are sensitive to ether and chloroform. Viruses are glycerol resistant, while formaldehyde, chlorine, and iodine are listed as inactivating agents.
optionExplanations: Correct. Ether and chloroform are listed as inactivating agents for enveloped viruses.
Incorrect. Viruses are glycerol resistant.
Incorrect. The lecture says they are sensitive to these agents.
Incorrect. Enveloped viruses are the ether-sensitive group.
questions.hint: Ether and chloroform point to the envelope.

questions.question: Which factor listed in the lecture affects viral tropism?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies specific receptors on target cells and required transcription factors as factors affecting viral tropism.
optionExplanations: Correct. Receptors allow attachment and entry into the target cell.
Incorrect. Blood group is not listed as the determining factor here.
Incorrect. Capsid color is not a tropism factor.
Incorrect. Laboratory temperature alone is not listed as a tropism factor.
questions.hint: Tropism begins with selective recognition of target cells.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly lists the six general steps of viral replication in the order given in the lecture?
options: Assembly → adsorption → release → penetration → uncoating → synthesis
Adsorption → penetration → uncoating → synthesis of viral macromolecules → assembly → release
Penetration → adsorption → synthesis → release → assembly → uncoating
Adsorption → assembly → penetration → uncoating → release → synthesis
questions.explanation: The six sequential steps are adsorption, penetration, uncoating, synthesis of viral macromolecules, assembly, and release.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The lecture places adsorption first and assembly later.
Correct. This is the exact order given.
Incorrect. The order of adsorption and later events is wrong.
Incorrect. Assembly does not occur immediately after adsorption.
questions.hint: Start with attachment and end with release.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a defective virus from a coreless virus?
options: A defective virus has an incomplete genome; a coreless virus has no nucleic-acid core
A defective virus has no capsid; a coreless virus has a complete genome
Both are complete mature viruses with complete genomes
A coreless virus can replicate with a helper virus
questions.explanation: A defective virus contains an incomplete genome and may replicate with a helper virus, whereas a coreless virus contains no nucleic-acid core and cannot infect or replicate.
optionExplanations: Correct. This matches the lecture definitions.
Incorrect. Defective viruses still have capsids.
Incorrect. Neither description matches the lecture.
Incorrect. Coreless viruses lack nucleic acid and cannot replicate even with a helper virus.
questions.hint: Compare what is inside the particle.

questions.question: Which chemical agents are viruses sensitive to according to the lecture?
Why is glycerol added to viral suspensions?
What is viral tropism?
options: The ability of a virus to survive drying
The ability of a virus to form a capsid
The ability of a virus to specifically infect a particular cell, tissue, or host that supports its replication
The ability of a virus to resist ultraviolet radiation

questions.question: Which two factors affect viral tropism?
options: Specific receptors and required transcription factors

questions.question: According to target organs, which classification is based on the site of viral infection?
options: Respiratory, gastrointestinal, urogenital, and hepatitis viruses

questions.question: Why does a virus require the machinery of a host cell for replication?
options: Because viruses contain no genetic material
Because viruses are metabolically inert and require cellular machinery for protein synthesis
Because viruses cannot attach to cells
Because viruses are unable to contain proteins

questions.question: Which cellular component provides the protein-synthesizing machinery required for viral replication?
Which molecule provides the energy required for protein synthesis during viral replication?
Which small biological precursors must the host cell provide for viral replication?
How does a virus redirect the host cell to produce viral-specific proteins?
options: Through viral mRNA, which is translated into viral-specific proteins

questions.question: Viral mRNA is synthesized by transcription of which viral genomes according to the lecture?
Which of the following is a structural viral protein?
Which of the following is a non-structural viral protein?
options: A viral enzyme involved in genome replication

questions.question: Which enzyme is carried as a virion component by retroviruses?
Which enzyme is carried by negative-sense RNA viruses as a virion component?
Which statement about the number of proteins encoded by viruses is correct?
options: All viruses encode exactly the same number of proteins
Small viruses always encode more proteins than large viruses
The number of proteins is unrelated to genome size
Large viruses can produce many proteins because they have larger genomes

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of the six major steps of viral replication?
options: Adsorption → penetration → uncoating → synthesis → assembly → release
Penetration → adsorption → synthesis → assembly → uncoating → release
Adsorption → synthesis → penetration → assembly → release → uncoating
Uncoating → adsorption → penetration → synthesis → release → assembly

questions.question: What is viral adsorption?
options: Release of viral particles from the host cell
Recognition and attachment of the virus to the host cell through viral attachment proteins binding to specific receptors
Separation of the viral genome from the capsid

questions.question: What do viral attachment proteins (VAPs) bind to during viral adsorption?
options: Specific protein or carbohydrate receptors on the host cell

questions.question: What is the term used for viral penetration by endocytosis?
How do non-enveloped viruses generally enter the host cell?
options: By direct genome injection into the nucleus

questions.question: During endocytosis of a non-enveloped virus, what is formed inside the host cell?
options: An endosomal vesicle containing the virus

questions.question: How can enveloped viruses enter a host cell according to the lecture?
In membrane fusion, what part of an enveloped virus is internalized into the host cell?
What is viral uncoating?
options: Separation of the viral genome from the outer viral structures
Attachment of the virus to the host receptor
Release of mature virions from the cell

questions.question: Where does the process of viral uncoating occur according to the lecture?
What happens to the infectivity of the internalized virus during uncoating?
options: It is abolished at this stage
It becomes independent of the host cell

questions.question: Where is the genome of most DNA viruses delivered after uncoating?
Which DNA virus is the exception whose genome remains in the cytoplasm?
Where does the genome of most RNA viruses remain after uncoating?
Which RNA virus group is the exception whose genome is delivered to the nucleus?
What is the stage of viral replication in which viral macromolecules are synthesized called?
Why is the synthesis stage called the eclipse phase?
options: Because the virus becomes visible under a microscope
Because no viral particles can be detected inside the infected host cell during this phase
Because the host cell immediately dies
Because the virus leaves the host cell

questions.question: What occurs during the eclipse phase?
options: The viral genome is transcribed and translated into proteins required for viral macromolecule synthesis
The virus attaches to the host receptor
The mature virus buds from the cell
The viral envelope is destroyed outside the cell

questions.question: What is produced during early transcription and translation?
options: Early viral proteins such as polymerases and regulatory proteins

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an early viral protein?
What is one major event occurring during late transcription and translation?
options: Initial attachment of the virus to the host cell

questions.question: Which type of proteins is synthesized during the late stage of transcription and translation?
options: Late viral proteins such as structural proteins and certain viral enzymes

questions.question: What is another term for viral assembly?
What happens during viral assembly?
options: All synthesized viral components irreversibly combine to form mature viral particles
The virus attaches to a host receptor
The host cell produces bacterial particles

questions.question: What does functional viral packaging mean?
options: Enclosing the complete viral genome inside its capsid
Removing the viral genome from the capsid
Replacing the viral genome with host DNA

questions.question: What can result from non-functional viral packaging?
options: Defective viruses, pseudoviruses, and coreless viruses

questions.question: What is a complete virus?

A fully mature virus containing a complete viral genome and capsid, with or without an envelope
A virus containing an incomplete viral genome

questions.question: What characterizes a defective virus?

It contains a complete viral genome and always replicates independently
It contains an incomplete viral genome and cannot replicate without a helper virus

questions.question: Which virus was given as an example of a defective virus?
Which virus is required as a helper virus for hepatitis D virus replication?
What is the process by which a defective virus is formed called?
What is a pseudovirus composed of?
options: A complete viral genome and capsid
Part of the host chromosome instead of viral nucleic acid, enclosed by a capsid with or without an envelope

questions.question: Why can a pseudovirus not replicate even in the presence of a helper virus?
options: It contains no viral nucleic acid
It cannot enter a host cell

questions.question: What is the process by which a pseudovirus is formed called?
What is a coreless virus?
options: A virus containing only viral RNA
A virus containing only host DNA
A particle composed only of capsid with or without an envelope and lacking a nucleic acid core
A virus containing an incomplete genome

questions.question: What is the ability of a coreless virus to infect or replicate?
options: It can infect and replicate normally
It can infect but cannot replicate
It can replicate but cannot infect

questions.question: What is the last step of the viral replication cycle?
By which two mechanisms can assembled viral particles be released from the infected cell?
How are non-enveloped (naked) viruses released from the infected cell?
options: By either budding or cell lysis

questions.question: When can an enveloped virus be released by budding according to the lecture?

When it has no nucleic acid
When it is a defective virus

questions.question: When can an enveloped virus be released by cell lysis according to the lecture?

When it contains only host DNA

A late stage in replication in which nucleocapsids acquire a membrane and are released as enveloped viruses
